verdict.reasoning: The semi-implicit generator (SIG) paper makes genuine but partial progress: it replaces discriminator-based adversarial training with a maximum-likelihood objective by modeling an explicit conditional layer over an implicit latent mixing distribution, trained by minimizing a Monte-Carlo upper bound on the cross-entropy. This gives a density-based training path for an implicit generative model, and it is shown to stabilize GANs when added as a regularizer. However, the paper itself states that the implicit mixing distribution p_φ(θ) cannot be evaluated pointwise and that the marginal P_model(x;φ) is implicit, so no explicit, closed-form density p_g(x) is produced; likelihood evaluation is only approximate (exact only as M→∞), and on complex data the method falls back to the adversarial GAN-SI framework. The second paper is a nonparametric convergence-rate analysis of noise-convolved VAE-type estimators and does not address the generator's missing explicit density — it even acknowledges the noiseless generator density may not exist. Thus the core of the gap — an explicit, evaluable density for the generator — remains open, though the likelihood-based training limitation has been meaningfully advanced.

paper.title: Semi-Implicit Generative Model
paper.abstract: To combine explicit and implicit generative models, we introduce semi-implicit generator (SIG) as a flexible hierarchical model that can be trained in the maximum likelihood framework. Both theoretically and experimentally, we demonstrate that SIG can generate high quality samples especially when dealing with multi-modality. By introducing SIG as an unbiased regularizer to the generative adversarial network (GAN), we show the interplay between maximum likelihood and adversarial learning can stabilize the adversarial training, resist the notorious mode collapsing problem of GANs, and improve the diversity of generated random samples.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes the semi-implicit generator (SIG), a hierarchical model x_i ~ p(x|θ_i) with an explicit conditional p(x|θ) and an implicit mixing distribution p_φ(θ) generated by a neural net transform. Because the conditional layer is explicit and the implicit θ can be MC-sampled, SIG can be trained in a maximum-likelihood framework by minimizing a Monte-Carlo upper bound H_M of the true cross-entropy (which converges to the true objective as M→∞), thereby giving a density-based training objective without a discriminator. The paper also adds SIG as a likelihood regularizer to GANs (GAN-SI), mainly to stabilize training and mitigate mode collapse.
assessments.what_remains_open: SIG does not actually provide an explicit, closed-form density p_g(x) for the generator: the paper explicitly states that p_φ(θ) cannot be evaluated pointwise and that the marginal P_model(x;φ) is implicit. Training is performed on an MC estimate / upper bound of the marginal likelihood (H ≥ H_{M+1} ≥ H_M, exact only in the M→∞ limit), so the model only offers approximate pointwise likelihood evaluation rather than an explicit density representation. Moreover, when scaled to complex data, the paper falls back on the adversarial framework (GAN-SI), which again relies on a discriminator and sample-based training; the main demonstrated benefit there is reduced mode collapse and stabilized optimization, not an explicit generator density. Thus the gap's specific problem — an explicit, evaluable density for the generator — remains unaddressed except in this semi-implicit, MC-estimated form.

paper.title: Minimax optimal density estimation using a shallow generative model with a one-dimensional latent variable
paper.abstract: A deep generative model yields an implicit estimator for the unknown distribution or density function of the observation. This paper investigates some statistical properties of the implicit density estimator pursued by VAE-type methods from a nonparametric density estimation framework. More specifically, we obtain convergence rates of the VAE-type density estimator under the assumption that the underlying true density function belongs to a locally Hölder class. Remarkably, a near minimax optimal rate with respect to the Hellinger metric can be achieved by the simplest network architecture, a shallow generative model with a one-dimensional latent variable.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper analyzes the statistical convergence rate of a VAE-type (likelihood-based) implicit density estimator built from ReLU generative models. Its estimated quantity is the noise-convolved density p_{g,σ}(x) = ∫ φ_σ(x − g(z)) dz, and it proves a near-minimax Hellinger rate n^{-β/(2β+d)} (up to log factors) for a sieve MLE over a shallow network class with a one-dimensional latent variable, with extensions to deep/composite generators. This is a nonparametric density-estimation theory contribution for likelihood-based generative models, not a treatment of the explicit-density limitation of generators.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — that the adversarial/generator framework yields no explicit density p_g(x) and only samples can be drawn from the generator — is not addressed. The paper studies VAE-type sieve MLE estimators and explicitly acknowledges that the density of g(Z) itself "may not exist"; it obtains a tractable likelihood only by adding Gaussian noise, so the (noiseless) generator distribution still has no explicit density representation. No GAN/adversarial estimator is considered, and no method is proposed to give an explicit p_g for generator outputs or to compute likelihoods of the generator distribution itself; that limitation remains exactly as stated in the gap.

verdict.reasoning: The subsequent literature makes real but narrow progress on the gap. One line of work approximates the intractable posterior expectation in the MLE gradient of a specific latent normalizing-flow/generator model via short-run Langevin dynamics, explicitly framing it as a perturbation of MLE rather than exact MLE. A second line handles permutation marginalization for autoregressive graph models, but exact likelihood is feasible only for very small graphs and larger cases rely on importance sampling. A third develops full-likelihood MLE for exponential-family graphical models with intractable normalizing constants, yet it depends fundamentally on the PEGM structure and breaks down when its variance/concentration conditions fail. A fourth contribution is purely theoretical, proving Jarzynski reweighting identities for EBM training but leaving weight variance, kernel selection, and practical scaling open. Notably, the EBM training paper does not make the intractable MLE computation tractable at all — it reinterprets the procedure as self-adversarial and sidesteps MLE. Thus several specific instances of the gap have been addressed, but no general method exists for the "many intractable probabilistic computations" the gap describes: partition functions, faithful sampling/mixing in high dimensions, continuous-latent marginal likelihoods, and practical estimator variance remain open. The verdict is partially solved with moderate confidence because the evidence is substantive but each assessment is scoped to one model family and one computation, with the broad problem still substantially open.

paper.title: A Tale of Two Latent Flows: Learning Latent Space Normalizing Flow with Short-run Langevin Flow for Approximate Inference
paper.abstract: We study a normalizing flow in the latent space of a top-down generator model, in which the normalizing flow model plays the role of the informative prior model of the generator. We propose to jointly learn the latent space normalizing flow prior model and the top-down generator model by a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)-based maximum likelihood algorithm, where a short-run Langevin sampling from the intractable posterior distribution is performed to infer the latent variables for each observed example, so that the parameters of the normalizing flow prior and the generator can be updated with the inferred latent variables. We show that, under the scenario of non-convergent short-run MCMC, the finite step Langevin dynamics is a flow-like approximate inference model and the learning objective actually follows the perturbation of the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). We further point out that the learning framework seeks to (i) match the latent space normalizing flow and the aggregated posterior produced by the short-run Langevin flow, and (ii) bias the model from MLE such that the short-run Langevin flow inference is close to the true posterior. Empirical results of extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed latent space normalizing flow model in the tasks of image generation, image reconstruction, anomaly detection, supervised image inpainting and unsupervised image recovery.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper tackles one specific intractable probabilistic computation that arises in MLE of a deep generative model: the expectation over the intractable posterior p(z|x) in the MLE gradient of a top-down generator with a normalizing-flow latent prior (LFBM). It approximates this posterior with a short-run (finite-step, non-convergent) Langevin dynamics, derives the resulting estimator as a perturbation of MLE with a KL-bias term that matches the prior to the aggregated Langevin posterior, and validates the approach empirically on generation, reconstruction, inpainting, anomaly detection, and incomplete-data recovery.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is broad — "many intractable probabilistic computations" arising in MLE and related strategies across deep generative models — whereas this paper addresses only one instance: posterior inference in a single model family (latent normalizing-flow prior + top-down generator), approximated by a biased, non-convergent short-run Langevin scheme. Other intractable MLE computations (e.g., partition functions of EBMs, exact marginal likelihoods of implicit/EBM generators, prior sampling for energy-based priors) are not solved; the method also inherits the limitation that the flow prior assumes latent variables are normalizable by invertible transformations, and the proposed approximation is only valid/derived under the short-run non-convergent MCMC scenario with a perturbation (KL-bias) from true MLE rather than an exact MLE solution. Thus the general challenge of approximating intractable computations in MLE remains open beyond this specific posterior-sampling setting.

paper.title: Order Matters: Probabilistic Modeling of Node Sequence for Graph Generation
paper.abstract: A graph generative model defines a distribution over graphs. One type of generative model is constructed by autoregressive neural networks, which sequentially add nodes and edges to generate a graph. However, the likelihood of a graph under the autoregressive model is intractable, as there are numerous sequences leading to the given graph; this makes maximum likelihood estimation challenging. Instead, in this work we derive the exact joint probability over the graph and the node ordering of the sequential process. From the joint, we approximately marginalize out the node orderings and compute a lower bound on the log-likelihood using variational inference. We train graph generative models by maximizing this bound, without using the ad-hoc node orderings of previous methods. Our experiments show that the log-likelihood bound is significantly tighter than the bound of previous schemes. Moreover, the models fitted with the proposed algorithm can generate high-quality graphs that match the structures of target graphs not seen during training. We have made our code publicly available at \hyperref[https://github.com/tufts-ml/graph-generation-vi]{https://github.com/tufts-ml/graph-generation-vi}.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper tackles a concrete instance of intractable computation in maximum likelihood estimation: for autoregressive graph generative models, the model likelihood requires marginalizing over node permutations, which is intractable. It addresses this by learning node orderings with an inference network (amortized proposal distribution) and by developing procedures to evaluate log-likelihood: exact enumeration of node permutations for small graphs, importance sampling with the learned proposal q for larger graphs, and Nauty/color-refinement based counting of permutations that lead to the same generated graph. The reviewer-response text positions these log-likelihood computations (exact and approximate) as key contributions enabling graph learning tasks that require likelihoods.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper only solves the permutation-marginalization intractability for one specific model class (autoregressive generative models of small/medium graphs). It does not provide general methods for the broad family of intractable probabilistic computations in MLE for deep generative models (e.g., posterior inference / ELBO gaps in VAEs, partition functions in energy-based models, intractable normalizing constants generally), and its own treatment remains approximate or limited: exact log-likelihood is only feasible for graphs under ~10 nodes, larger graphs rely on importance sampling whose quality depends on the learned proposal, and the permutation-counting step requires external canonicalization tools (Nauty). The gap's broad claim that intractable MLE computations limit deep generative models' impact is therefore only partially addressed within this narrow domain.

paper.title: EBMs Trained with Maximum Likelihood are Generator Models Trained with a Self-adverserial Loss
paper.abstract: Maximum likelihood estimation is widely used in training Energy-based models (EBMs). Training requires samples from an unnormalized distribution, which is usually intractable, and in practice, these are obtained by MCMC algorithms such as Langevin dynamics. However, since MCMC in high-dimensional space converges extremely slowly, the current understanding of maximum likelihood training, which assumes approximate samples from the model can be drawn, is problematic. In this paper, we try to understand this training procedure by replacing Langevin dynamics with deterministic solutions of the associated gradient descent ODE. Doing so allows us to study the density induced by the dynamics (if the dynamics are invertible), and connect with GANs by treating the dynamics as generator models, the initial values as latent variables and the loss as optimizing a critic defined by the very same energy that determines the generator through its gradient. Hence the term - self-adversarial loss. We show that reintroducing the noise in the dynamics does not lead to a qualitative change in the behavior, and merely reduces the quality of the generator. We thus show that EBM training is effectively a self-adversarial procedure rather than maximum likelihood estimation.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper targets the specific intractable computation in EBM maximum likelihood training: drawing negative samples from the unnormalized model density p_theta(x), normally done by slowly-converging MCMC/Langevin dynamics. It replaces Langevin sampling with the deterministic (noise-free) gradient-descent ODE, treats the resulting invertible dynamics as a generator/flow model with tractable likelihood via the change-of-variables formula, and shows empirically that the density induced by the dynamics matches the data while the EBM's own density does not. It then draws a connection to WGANs, adding a self-adversarial/generator loss term that improves sample quality and training stability on toy and image data. This bears on the gap by providing an alternative training route that avoids the intractable model-sampling step, rather than making that sampling tractable.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not actually solve the intractable probabilistic computations that maximum likelihood estimation requires. It concludes that EBM training "is effectively a self-adversarial procedure rather than maximum likelihood estimation," i.e., it abandons the MLE interpretation instead of computing the intractable expectation under p_theta or the partition function Z_theta. Its remedy is limited in scope: it requires noise-free, invertible dynamics (mild Lipschitz conditions and small step sizes for invertibility), finite short-run steps with Gaussian initialization, relatively simple convolutional energy networks, and image settings where it only compares relative FID quality. It does not address other intractable computations that arise in MLE of deep generative models (e.g., partition functions, exact sampling from the true model density, faithful MCMC mixing in high dimensions), nor does it provide a general method for making MLE's intractable computations tractable. The claims about avoiding the sampling bottleneck are empirical and tied to these specific models.

paper.title: Likelihood Based Inference in Fully and Partially Observed Exponential Family Graphical Models with Intractable Normalizing Constants
paper.abstract: Probabilistic graphical models that encode an underlying Markov random field are fundamental building blocks of generative modeling to learn latent representations in modern multivariate data sets with complex dependency structures. Among these, the exponential family graphical models are especially popular, given their fairly well-understood statistical properties and computational scalability to high-dimensional data based on pseudo-likelihood methods. These models have been successfully applied in many fields, such as the Ising model in statistical physics and count graphical models in genomics. Another strand of models allows some nodes to be latent, so as to allow the marginal distribution of the observable nodes to depart from exponential family to capture more complex dependence. These approaches form the basis of generative models in artificial intelligence, such as the Boltzmann machines and their restricted versions. A fundamental barrier to likelihood-based (i.e., both maximum likelihood and fully Bayesian) inference in both fully and partially observed cases is the intractability of the likelihood. The usual workaround is via adopting pseudo-likelihood based approaches, following the pioneering work of Besag (1974). The goal of this paper is to demonstrate that full likelihood based analysis of these models is feasible in a computationally efficient manner. The chief innovation lies in using a technique of Geyer (1991) utilizing the tractable independence model underlying an intractable graphical model, to estimate the normalizing constant, as well as its gradient. Extensive numerical results, supporting theory and comparisons with pseudo-likelihood based approaches demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper tackles precisely the class of intractable MLE computations caused by intractable normalizing constants in deep generative models built on exponential-family/Markov-random-field architectures. It develops a computationally efficient full-likelihood procedure (MLE, penalized MLE, and Bayesian HMC) for fully observed pairwise exponential family graphical models (Ising, Poisson, etc.) and for partially observed latent-variable versions (RBM, DBM, and full Boltzmann machines without bipartite restrictions), estimating z(θ) and its gradient by importance sampling from the tractable independence model φ = diag(θ), which allows cheap i.i.d. batch sampling instead of per-update MCMC/CD. It provides theory (bounded variance under stated conditions, sub-Gaussian concentration for finite-support PEGMs, sample-size scaling under logarithmic sparsity) and numerical comparisons against pseudo-likelihood and contrastive divergence.
assessments.what_remains_open: The solution is scoped to one family of deep generative models and one kind of intractable computation. First, it relies fundamentally on the exponential-family graphical model (PEGM) structure: the method requires that the independence-model normalizing constant z(diag(θ)) is available in closed form and that i.i.d. sampling from the independence model is cheap, so it does not address other intractable probabilistic computations that arise in MLE of other deep generative models (e.g., continuous-latent marginal likelihoods/ELBO-style inference in VAEs, likelihoods of diffusion or flow-based models). Second, even within this family the guarantees hold only under conditions and can break down otherwise: bounded variance requires (2u+φ) ∈ Θ (and (2(1+δ)u+φ) ∈ Θ for the gradient estimate), exponential concentration requires bounded-support sample spaces, the O(p) sample size result assumes logarithmic sparsity, and the authors report catastrophic MSE degradation when these conditions are violated. Finally, the demonstration for the most ambitious target, training a full (unrestricted) Boltzmann machine, is empirically limited to small visible dimensions for the TV comparisons and to approximate evaluations at p=100, and the paper explicitly leaves a theoretical treatment of full-BM representational power as future work.

paper.title: Jarzynski Reweighting and Sampling Dynamics for Training Energy-Based Models: Theoretical Analysis of Different Transition Kernels
paper.abstract: Energy-Based Models (EBMs) provide a flexible framework for generative modeling, but their training remains theoretically challenging due to the need to approximate normalization constants and efficiently sample from complex, multi-modal distributions. Traditional methods, such as contrastive divergence and score matching, introduce biases that can hinder accurate learning. In this work, we present a theoretical analysis of Jarzynski reweighting, a technique from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, and its implications for training EBMs. We focus on the role of the choice of the kernel and we illustrate these theoretical considerations in two key generative frameworks: (i) flow-based diffusion models, where we reinterpret Jarzynski reweighting in the context of stochastic interpolants to mitigate discretization errors and improve sample quality, and (ii) Restricted Boltzmann Machines, where we analyze its role in correcting the biases of contrastive divergence. Our results provide insights into the interplay between kernel choice and model performance, highlighting the potential of Jarzynski reweighting as a principled tool for generative learning.

verdict.reasoning: All five papers are partial mitigations rather than direct solutions, and collectively they cover pieces of the gap but leave meaningful substance open. Unbalanced GANs stabilizes only early-epoch balance via VAE pretraining and still runs the standard unmodified objective afterward, while actually increasing architecture burden (a matched VAE is required). COEGAN and CDE-GAN automate or coordinate some training/architecture choices and report reduced mode collapse, but COEGAN itself notes mode collapse still occurs in some runs and quality lags far behind hand-designed baselines, while CDE-GAN keeps fixed hand-designed architectures and offers only a heuristic balance mechanism with no theoretical guarantee. IGAN targets stability/mode collapse but only at 64x64 on limited datasets, does not directly measure mode coverage, and still relies on a carefully hand-crafted architecture/regularization recipe. MR-GAN provides the strongest theoretical foothold (generalization bound, epsilon-equilibrium, local stability) and avoids mode collapse on a toy mixture, but only demonstrates local stability, introduces new sensitive hyperparameters, and does not remove architecture sensitivity. Together these papers substantially mitigate training instability and mode dropping in specific settings, but none removes the need for careful balance or careful architecture design, and mode dropping is neither generally solved nor guaranteed. Hence the gap is partially, not fully, addressed.

paper.title: Unbalanced GANs: Pre-training the Generator of Generative Adversarial Network using Variational Autoencoder
paper.abstract: We propose Unbalanced GANs, which pre-trains the generator of the generative adversarial network (GAN) using variational autoencoder (VAE). We guarantee the stable training of the generator by preventing the faster convergence of the discriminator at early epochs. Furthermore, we balance between the generator and the discriminator at early epochs and thus maintain the stabilized training of GANs. We apply Unbalanced GANs to well known public datasets and find that Unbalanced GANs reduce mode collapses. We also show that Unbalanced GANs outperform ordinary GANs in terms of stabilized learning, faster convergence and better image quality at early epochs.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Unbalanced GANs, which pre-trains the GAN generator by transferring the weights of a VAE's variational decoder (built with the same architecture as the target generator), and then trains the ordinary GAN objective. This initialization prevents the discriminator from converging faster than the generator at early epochs, which the authors argue stabilizes training, speeds convergence, improves early-epoch image quality, and empirically reduces mode collapse on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and LSUN Bedroom for DCGAN/LSGAN/WGAN backbones.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's three parts are only partially covered. (1) Balance: the paper only equalizes generator/discriminator strength at initialization/early epochs via a good starting point; after that it runs the standard unmodified min-max objective, so it offers no online balance-enforcing mechanism for later training (unlike BEGAN's equilibrium control), and the underlying balance fragility remains. (2) Mode dropping: the paper only shows mode collapse is reduced/avoided on the tested image datasets, not solved or guaranteed; the experiments are qualitative or rely on Inception Score at early epochs. (3) Architecture design: the method does not remove the need for careful architecture design — on the contrary, it requires constructing an additional VAE whose decoder/encoder match the target GAN's architecture, and the authors even acknowledge the benefit shrinks on the larger LSUN dataset ("standard deviations of losses ... have almost no differences ... the speed of convergence made no great difference"). Thus the paper is a mitigation under specific conditions (image GANs with a compatible VAE pretrained per dataset) rather than a general solution to careful-balance/architecture/mode-dropping difficulties.

paper.title: Coevolution of Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GAN) became a hot topic, presenting impressive results in the field of computer vision. However, there are still open problems with the GAN model, such as the training stability and the hand-design of architectures. Neuroevolution is a technique that can be used to provide the automatic design of network architectures even in large search spaces as in deep neural networks. Therefore, this project proposes COEGAN, a model that combines neuroevolution and coevolution in the coordination of the GAN training algorithm. The proposal uses the adversarial characteristic between the generator and discriminator components to design an algorithm using coevolution techniques. Our proposal was evaluated in the MNIST dataset. The results suggest the improvement of the training stability and the automatic discovery of efficient network architectures for GANs. Our model also partially solves the mode collapse problem.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes COEGAN, which combines neuroevolution (DeepNEAT-based) and competitive coevolution to train GANs by evolving the architectures of both generators and discriminators automatically. On MNIST, the authors report that all runs converged with equilibrium between generator and discriminator (no vanishing gradient), automatic discovery of architectures, and partial mitigation of mode collapse. This bears directly on the gap because it targets automatic architecture design and the generator/discriminator balance problem through a coevolutionary coordination of training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper only partially solves the gap, and says so itself. Mode dropping/mode collapse is only partially addressed: "For some executions, the generator captured only a subset of the distribution, which is a form of the mode collapse problem." In addition, the evolved models do not match hand-designed state-of-the-art quality (mean FID 49.2 vs. 6.7 reported elsewhere), so automatic architecture design is demonstrated only on MNIST with small populations and a 4-layer genome limit, and the discriminator fitness (loss) is acknowledged as noisy and needing improvement. Balance is eased but not removed — it is shifted to evolutionary choices (k-best pairing, FID fitness for generators) rather than fully solved, and no evidence is given for larger datasets or broader settings.

paper.title: IGAN: A New Inception-based Model for Stable and High-Fidelity Image Synthesis Using Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) face a significant challenge of striking an optimal balance between high-quality image generation and training stability. Recent techniques, such as DCGAN, BigGAN, and StyleGAN, improve visual fidelity; however, such techniques usually struggle with mode collapse and unstable gradients at high network depth. This paper proposes a novel GAN structural model that incorporates deeper inception-inspired convolution and dilated convolution. This novel model is termed the Inception Generative Adversarial Network (IGAN). The IGAN model generates high-quality synthetic images while maintaining training stability, by reducing mode collapse as well as preventing vanishing and exploding gradients. Our proposed IGAN model achieves the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) of 13.12 and 15.08 on the CUB-200 and ImageNet datasets, respectively, representing a 28-33% improvement in FID over the state-of-the-art GANs. Additionally, the IGAN model attains an Inception Score (IS) of 9.27 and 68.25, reflecting improved image diversity and generation quality. Finally, the two techniques of dropout and spectral normalization are utilized in both the generator and discriminator structures to further mitigate gradient explosion and overfitting. These findings confirm that the IGAN model potentially balances training stability with image generation quality, constituting a scalable and computationally efficient framework for high-fidelity image synthesis.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes IGAN, a modified GAN architecture whose generator and discriminator use inception-style modules with parallel 1×1, 3×3, and dilated 5×5 convolutions plus average pooling, combined with spectral normalization, dropout, and batch normalization in both networks. The stated aim is exactly to overcome mode collapse and training instability (vanishing/exploding gradients) while maintaining high-fidelity generation, and the authors report improved FID (13.12 CUB-200, 15.08 ImageNet) and IS over BigGAN/SNGAN/SAGAN baselines, along with loss curves that stabilize over 500 epochs.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is a broad, open-ended claim about standard GANs, and IGAN only mitigates it under narrow conditions rather than removing it. The gap's core problem — that GAN training still requires careful balance and careful architecture design and still suffers mode dropping — is only partially addressed: (1) results are demonstrated only at low 64×64 resolution on CUB-200 and a 20-category subset of ImageNet that is itself trained per-category/small-data, so scalability to large-scale and high-resolution generation is not established; (2) mode dropping is not directly measured (only IS/quality proxies are reported), and the paper does not supply a controlled mode-coverage or collapse experiment against baselines under identical conditions; (3) the architecture does not eliminate careful design or tuning — stability is bought by a specific hand-crafted module plus spectral normalization and dropout, and FID comparisons against baselines use values taken from reference papers rather than re-trained baselines, so the claimed improvement over 'standard GAN balance' is not rigorously controlled. Thus the underlying problems (mode dropping still possible, and a new careful architecture/regularization recipe is still required) remain open.

paper.title: CDE-GAN: Cooperative Dual Evolution Based Generative Adversarial Network
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have been a popular deep generative model for real-world applications. Despite many recent efforts on GANs that have been contributed, mode collapse and instability of GANs are still open problems caused by their adversarial optimization difficulties. In this paper, motivated by the cooperative co-evolutionary algorithm, we propose a Cooperative Dual Evolution based Generative Adversarial Network (CDE-GAN) to circumvent these drawbacks. In essence, CDE-GAN incorporates dual evolution with respect to the generator(s) and discriminators into a unified evolutionary adversarial framework to conduct effective adversarial multi-objective optimization. Thus it exploits the complementary properties and injects dual mutation diversity into training to steadily diversify the estimated density in capturing multi-modes and improve generative performance. Specifically, CDE-GAN decomposes the complex adversarial optimization problem into two subproblems (generation and discrimination), and each subproblem is solved with a separated subpopulation (E-Generator} and E-Discriminators), evolved by its own evolutionary algorithm. Additionally, we further propose a Soft Mechanism to balance the trade-off between E-Generators and E-Discriminators to conduct steady training for CDE-GAN. Extensive experiments on one synthetic dataset and three real-world benchmark image datasets demonstrate that the proposed CDE-GAN achieves a competitive and superior performance in generating good quality and diverse samples over baselines. The code and more generated results are available at our project homepage: https://shiming-chen.github.io/CDE-GAN-website/CDE-GAN.html.

assessments.contribution_summary: CDE-GAN targets two of the three stated GAN problems: unstable/balance-sensitive adversarial training and mode collapse/mode dropping. It decomposes the adversarial game into two subproblems solved by co-evolved subpopulations (E-Generators with three mutation objectives and E-Discriminators with two), uses quality+diversity fitness and survivor selection, and adds a "Soft Mechanism" that softens discriminator maximization (softmax over multiple discriminators, delta=1) to keep generator/discriminator balance. Experiments on a synthetic 8-Gaussian mixture and CIFAR-10/LSUN/CelebA report better stability and Inception Score than baselines including E-GAN, arguing that dual evolution diversifies the density estimate to cover multiple modes.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the "careful network architecture design" facet of the gap: CDE-GAN still trains fixed, hand-designed DCGAN-style architectures and provides no mechanism to relax architectural sensitivity or automate architecture design. Mode dropping is mitigated but not generally solved — the evidence is empirical on limited datasets (2D 8-Gaussian, CIFAR-10, LSUN-Bedrooms, CelebA) with no theoretical coverage guarantee, and the authors acknowledge added per-iteration cost. Balance is handled by a specific heuristic (softmax weighting with a fixed delta=1 over an ensemble of discriminators) rather than a principled guarantee of stable equilibrium, so the careful-balance problem is reduced, not eliminated.

paper.title: MR-GAN: Manifold Regularized Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Despite the growing interest in generative adversarial networks (GANs), training GANs remains a challenging problem, both from a theoretical and a practical standpoint. To address this challenge, in this paper, we propose a novel way to exploit the unique geometry of the real data, especially the manifold information. More specifically, we design a method to regularize GAN training by adding an additional regularization term referred to as manifold regularizer. The manifold regularizer forces the generator to respect the unique geometry of the real data manifold and generate high quality data. Furthermore, we theoretically prove that the addition of this regularization term in any class of GANs including DCGAN and Wasserstein GAN leads to improved performance in terms of generalization, existence of equilibrium, and stability. Preliminary experiments show that the proposed manifold regularization helps in avoiding mode collapse and leads to stable training.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes MR-GAN, which adds a manifold regularizer to the generator's update so that the generated distribution is forced to respect the geometry of the real-data manifold. It claims to overcome the standard GAN failure modes of mode collapse, lack of equilibrium, and instability: it proves a generalization bound, existence of an ε-approximate equilibrium, and local exponential stability for any GAN class (including DCGAN and WGAN) with the added regularizer, and reports experiments showing that MR-GAN avoids mode collapse on a toy 2D mixture of Gaussians and improves Geometry Scores over WGAN/DCGAN baselines on MNIST and CelebA.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns the whole bundle of difficulties in standard GAN training: careful generator/discriminator balance, careful architecture design, and mode dropping. The paper addresses only part of this. Mode-collapse avoidance is demonstrated empirically only on a small toy dataset; on MNIST/CelebA the evidence is improved Geometry Scores rather than direct demonstration of full mode coverage, and the improvements occur only for small values of the regularization parameter λ (larger λ degrades results), so the method introduces new sensitive hyperparameters (λ, kernel scale ρ) and a new design choice (embedding function ψ, e.g., an autoencoder) rather than removing the need for careful tuning/architecture design. The stability result is only local exponential stability around an equilibrium; the paper itself states that global convergence properties remain open. Thus it mitigates instability and mode dropping in limited settings but does not fully solve the balance/architecture-design sensitivity or mode-dropping problem in general.

paper.title: The boundary method for semi-discrete optimal transport partitions and Wasserstein distance computation
paper.abstract: We introduce a new technique, which we call the boundary method, for solving semi-discrete optimal transport problems with a wide range of cost functions. The boundary method reduces the effective dimension of the problem, thus improving complexity. For cost functions equal to a p-norm with p in (1,infinity), we provide mathematical justification, convergence analysis, and algorithmic development. Our testing supports the boundary method with these p-norms, as well as other, more general cost functions.

paper.title: Optimal Transport Flow Matching by Design
paper.abstract: Flow matching models learn to transport samples from a simple prior distribution to a complex data distribution. When prior-data pairs are coupled via optimal transport (OT), the learned trajectories are straight and non-crossing, enabling fast, even single-step, generation. However, computing the OT coupling in high dimensions is intractable, and existing methods attempt to solve the OT problem, at the cost of persistent bias or significant overhead. Rather than solving for the OT coupling, we reformulate the problem. Once the prior is treated as a design choice rather than a fixed input, the OT coupling between prior and data is no longer unique. Many priors admit an OT-optimal identity coupling to the data, leaving us free to choose one that is also tractable to sample. We identify low-frequency projection of natural images as such a choice. The identity coupling between data and its low-frequency representation is empirically OT-optimal, the prior is structured enough to be sampled by a lightweight model at inference, and the remaining flow-matching task reduces to synthesizing high-frequency detail. Interpolating the prior with Gaussian noise further improves generation quality while preserving the OT coupling. The approach requires no modifications to the flow model itself, and integrates naturally with latent-space models, classifier-free guidance, and one-step generation frameworks. Across all benchmarks, our method reduces trajectory curvature by more than $2\times$ compared to existing flow matching methods, yielding better generation quality in the few-step regime.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper addresses a different OT intractability: computing the OT *coupling* between a Gaussian prior and data for flow matching. It proposes "OT by design" — replacing the fixed Gaussian prior with a low-frequency projection prior whose identity coupling to the data is (empirically) OT-optimal, thereby avoiding any OT solver and yielding straighter trajectories and better few-step generation. It does not compute, estimate, or bound the Wasserstein/EM distance between distributions, and it does not engage with the Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual at all.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem is the intractability of computing the EM/Wasserstein distance value, whose primal definition is an infimum over couplings and which is normally approximated via the Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual (e.g., in WGAN-style estimation). This paper never computes or approximates a Wasserstein/EM distance, never discusses the KR dual, and proposes no alternative for evaluating the distance between two arbitrary distributions. Its "OT-optimality" claims concern the discrete Monge coupling (identity pairing) used to train a generative flow, verified with the Hungarian algorithm, not the value of an EM distance. Therefore the intractability of the Wasserstein-distance infimum and its dual-based approximation remain entirely open after this work.

paper.title: Entropic regularization of continuous optimal transport problems
paper.abstract: We analyze continuous optimal transport problems in the so-called Kantorovich form, where we seek a transport plan between two marginals that are probability measures on compact subsets of Euclidean space. We consider the case of regularization with the negative entropy with respect to the Lebesgue measure, which has attracted attention because it can be solved by the very simple Sinkhorn algorithm. We first analyze the regularized problem in the context of classical Fenchel duality and derive a strong duality result for a predual problem in the space of continuous functions. However, this problem may not admit a minimizer, which prevents obtaining primal-dual optimality conditions. We then show that the primal problem is naturally analyzed in the Orlicz space of functions with finite entropy in the sense that the entropically regularized problem admits a minimizer if and only if the marginals have finite entropy. We then derive a dual problem in the corresponding dual space, for which existence can be shown by purely variational arguments and primal-dual optimality conditions can be derived. For marginals that do not have finite entropy, we finally show Gamma-convergence of the regularized problem with smoothed marginals to the original Kantorovich problem.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper studies the entropically regularized Kantorovich (optimal transport) problem in the continuous setting, rather than the unregularized Wasserstein/EM distance. It proves strong Fenchel duality between the regularized primal and a continuous-function predual, shows that a regularized primal minimizer exists iff the marginals have finite entropy (lie in the Orlicz space Llog), derives an Lexp-valued dual with existence of maximizers and primal-dual optimality conditions that can underpin the Sinkhorn iteration, and finally establishes Gamma-convergence of regularized problems with smoothed marginals to the original (unregularized) Kantorovich problem.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns the specific intractability of the Wasserstein/EM distance infimum over couplings and the Kantorovich-Rubinstein dual approximation used to bypass it. This paper neither addresses the intractability of that primal infimum nor analyzes the KR dual of the original unregularized problem as a computable surrogate. Instead, it changes the problem via negative-entropy regularization (a different tractability route leading to Sinkhorn-type methods for the regularized surrogate) and focuses on well-posedness, duality, and Gamma-convergence theory. It provides no treatment of computing the actual Wasserstein distance or of the KR dual approximation, so the stated gap remains open in this paper.

paper.title: Optimal transport with $f$-divergence regularization and generalized Sinkhorn algorithm
paper.abstract: Entropic regularization provides a generalization of the original optimal transport problem. It introduces a penalty term defined by the Kullback-Leibler divergence, making the problem more tractable via the celebrated Sinkhorn algorithm. Replacing the Kullback-Leibler divergence with a general $f$-divergence leads to a natural generalization. The case of divergences defined by superlinear functions was recently studied by Di Marino and Gerolin. Using convex analysis, we extend the theory developed so far to include all $f$-divergences defined by functions of Legendre type, and prove that under some mild conditions, strong duality holds, optimums in both the primal and dual problems are attained, the generalization of the $c$-transform is well-defined, and we give sufficient conditions for the generalized Sinkhorn algorithm to converge to an optimal solution. We propose a practical algorithm for computing an approximate solution of the optimal transport problem with $f$-divergence regularization via the generalized Sinkhorn algorithm. Finally, we present experimental results on synthetic 2-dimensional data, demonstrating the effects of using different $f$-divergences for regularization, which influences convergence speed, numerical stability and sparsity of the optimal coupling.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper deals with tractability of an OT problem whose primal is an infimum over couplings, but only in its *regularized* form OT_ε with a general f-divergence penalty, not the Wasserstein/EM distance itself. It proves strong duality (primal infimum = dual supremum), existence/attainment of optima, a generalized (c,ε,φ)-transform, and convergence of a generalized Sinkhorn algorithm under mild assumptions, together with a practical parallel implementation. This shows that for the ε-regularized surrogate, the infimum over couplings can be avoided and solved via the dual/Sinkhorn iterations.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific target — the exact, unregularized Wasserstein (EM) distance infimum over couplings, and its Kantorovich-Rubinstein dual approximation — is not solved. All main results are for ε > 0 (the ε = 0 case is only mentioned as the classical limit, not analyzed). Consequently the paper provides no tractable exact computation of the Wasserstein distance and no guarantee that its regularized value approximates the true EM distance as ε → 0 in this generalized f-divergence setting (no Γ-convergence/error bounds are established; such results are only cited for the KL case). Moreover, the regularized optimum is explicitly biased away from the true OT coupling, and the algorithmic guarantees require restrictive conditions (φ of Legendre type, compact/full-support spaces, Lipschitz setting, and for non-superlinear divergences a "good triple" hypothesis).

paper.title: Estimating Convergence of Markov chains with L-Lag Couplings
paper.abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods generate samples that are asymptotically distributed from a target distribution of interest as the number of iterations goes to infinity. Various theoretical results provide upper bounds on the distance between the target and marginal distribution after a fixed number of iterations. These upper bounds are on a case by case basis and typically involve intractable quantities, which limits their use for practitioners. We introduce L-lag couplings to generate computable, non-asymptotic upper bound estimates for the total variation or the Wasserstein distance of general Markov chains. We apply L-lag couplings to the tasks of (i) determining MCMC burn-in, (ii) comparing different MCMC algorithms with the same target, and (iii) comparing exact and approximate MCMC. Lastly, we (iv) assess the bias of sequential Monte Carlo and self-normalized importance samplers.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper introduces L-lag couplings of two Markov chains to obtain computable, simulation-based non-asymptotic upper bound estimates of integral probability metrics — including total variation and 1-Wasserstein distance — between a chain's marginal π_t and its invariant distribution π (Theorem 1 gives d_H(π_t,π) ≤ E[Σ_j M_H(X_{t+jL}, Y_{t+(j-1)L})]). Since it estimates the 1-Wasserstein distance without ever computing the infimum over transport couplings, it is a coupling/simulation-based workaround for Wasserstein-distance intractability, applied to MCMC burn-in, algorithm comparison, mixing-time comparison (ULA vs MALA), and SMC/self-normalized importance bias.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns the general intractability of the Wasserstein (EM) distance defined as an infimum over couplings. This paper does not make the exact Wasserstein distance computable: it produces only non-tight UPPER BOUNDS (empirical estimates of the expectation in Theorem 1), applicable in the narrow special setting of the distance between a Markov chain marginal and its stationary distribution. It relies on restrictive conditions (ability to construct faithful, meeting-in-finite-time joint kernels; Assumptions 1–3 on moment bounds, sub-exponential meeting-time tails, and faithfulness) and its bounds are explicitly loose because "the couplings considered in this work are chosen to be widely applicable but are not optimal in any way." It also says "since the proposed upper bounds are not tight, the true convergence rates ... may be ordered differently." The exact optimal-transport infimum, and an exact or dual-based (Kantorovich–Rubinstein) computation of Wasserstein distance between general measures, remain unaddressed; the paper provides no lower bounds or exact distance evaluation and offers no computable scheme for arbitrary pairs of distributions, only for π_t vs π in MCMC settings.

paper.title: Wasserstein GANs Work Because They Fail (to Approximate the Wasserstein Distance)
paper.abstract: Wasserstein GANs are based on the idea of minimising the Wasserstein distance between a real and a generated distribution. We provide an in-depth mathematical analysis of differences between the theoretical setup and the reality of training Wasserstein GANs. In this work, we gather both theoretical and empirical evidence that the WGAN loss is not a meaningful approximation of the Wasserstein distance. Moreover, we argue that the Wasserstein distance is not even a desirable loss function for deep generative models, and conclude that the success of Wasserstein GANs can in truth be attributed to a failure to approximate the Wasserstein distance.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly probes the WGAN modeling assumption that the Kantorovich-Rubinstein supremum (Kantorovich's potential) is attained/well-approximated by the parameterized critic. It shows theoretically and empirically that the WGAN-GP loss is not an accurate approximation of the distributional Wasserstein distance because the inner-loop discriminator fails to capture the optimal critic (e.g., normalized estimates are an order of magnitude off even for static distributions trained for 300K iterations), and that even when the batch supremum is attained accurately (c-transform WGAN), generative quality degrades. It concludes that the critic does not attain the KR supremum in practice and argues this failure — rather than Wasserstein minimization — explains WGAN success, attributing it instead to Lipschitz regularization.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper validates the "strong assumption" criticism empirically and argues the attainment failure is beneficial, but it does not provide a rigorous theoretical treatment of critic-family attainability: there are no formal conditions, convergence/approximation guarantees, or bounds characterizing when a parameterized critic can or cannot attain the KR supremum. Its evidence is empirical and confined to specific setups (static CIFAR-10 pairs, an 8-mode Gaussian, CelebA), and the recommendation is to stop viewing WGANs as Wasserstein minimizers rather than to repair or replace the theoretical derivation that relies on the assumption. A full resolution of the gap would need a formal analysis or a revised WGAN derivation that does not hinge on supremum attainment.

paper.title: GraN-GAN: Piecewise Gradient Normalization for Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Modern generative adversarial networks (GANs) predominantly use piecewise linear activation functions in discriminators (or critics), including ReLU and LeakyReLU. Such models learn piecewise linear mappings, where each piece handles a subset of the input space, and the gradients per subset are piecewise constant. Under such a class of discriminator (or critic) functions, we present Gradient Normalization (GraN), a novel input-dependent normalization method, which guarantees a piecewise K-Lipschitz constraint in the input space. In contrast to spectral normalization, GraN does not constrain processing at the individual network layers, and, unlike gradient penalties, strictly enforces a piecewise Lipschitz constraint almost everywhere. Empirically, we demonstrate improved image generation performance across multiple datasets (incl. CIFAR-10/100, STL-10, LSUN bedrooms, and CelebA), GAN loss functions, and metrics. Further, we analyze altering the often untuned Lipschitz constant K in several standard GANs, not only attaining significant performance gains, but also finding connections between K and training dynamics, particularly in low-gradient loss plateaus, with the common Adam optimizer.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper tackles a concrete piecewise-linear-unit difficulty inside a generative model: GAN discriminators/critics built from ReLU/LeakyReLU are piecewise linear, giving piecewise-constant input gradients whose norms are uncontrolled, which destabilizes generator training. It proposes Gradient Normalization (GraN), which multiplies the (piecewise linear) scalar discriminator/critic output by a function of its local gradient norm, enforcing a piecewise K-Lipschitz constraint with constant-norm (≈K) gradients almost everywhere, and thereby bounds the gradients received by the generator (‖∇_x L_G‖ ≤ K). Extensive image-generation experiments (CIFAR-10/100, STL-10, LSUN, CelebA) across loss functions and metrics show competitive or improved FID/IS/KID versus gradient-penalty and spectral-normalization baselines.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns difficulty of leveraging piecewise linear units in generative models broadly. The paper only addresses one slice of this: the discriminator/critic side of unconditional GANs (and only scalar-output, piecewise-linear-activation networks). It does not address piecewise linear activations inside the generator itself, nor other generative-model families (VAEs, flow/score/diffusion/autoregressive) where piecewise linear units' well-behaved gradients might be hard to exploit in the generative direction. It also does not investigate leveraging piecewise linearity for the benefit of sampling/representation in the generator; rather it constrains the discriminator to make GAN training stable.

paper.title: Activation-Descent Regularization for Input Optimization of ReLU Networks
paper.abstract: We present a new approach for input optimization of ReLU networks that explicitly takes into account the effect of changes in activation patterns. We analyze local optimization steps in both the input space and the space of activation patterns to propose methods with superior local descent properties. To accomplish this, we convert the discrete space of activation patterns into differentiable representations and propose regularization terms that improve each descent step. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed input-optimization methods for improving the state-of-the-art in various areas, such as adversarial learning, generative modeling, and reinforcement learning.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper targets the underlying cause of the gap in one specific setting: it develops ADR-GD, an input-optimization method for ReLU networks that explicitly models changes in activation patterns (via differentiable sigmoid-surrogate activation variables, constraint losses, and perturbed gradient descent). It demonstrates this in generative-model use, specifically latent-variable optimization / reconstructing target images with pretrained ReLU-based generators, as one of several applications (also adversarial attacks and DRL action optimization). Thus it improves one workflow where piecewise-linear activations hurt generative optimization.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper only attacks a narrow, indirect facet of the gap: input/latent-space optimization through an already-trained ReLU generator. It does not address the broader problem of generative models "leveraging the benefits of piecewise linear units" in training or design — e.g., dead-ReLU/vanishing-gradient difficulties during GAN or likelihood-based training of ReLU generators, why piecewise linear units work well discriminatively but poorly generatively, or architectural/learning changes to make ReLU-based generative training robust. Generative modeling is a secondary application of a general ReLU input-optimizer; the paper proposes no generative-specific solution, and the generative experiments (image reconstruction via latent optimization) are largely relegated to benchmarks with the core contribution framed around adversarial attacks and general ReLU optimization.

paper.title: Soft-Root-Sign Activation Function
paper.abstract: The choice of activation function in deep networks has a significant effect on the training dynamics and task performance. At present, the most effective and widely-used activation function is ReLU. However, because of the non-zero mean, negative missing and unbounded output, ReLU is at a potential disadvantage during optimization. To this end, we introduce a novel activation function to manage to overcome the above three challenges. The proposed nonlinearity, namely "Soft-Root-Sign" (SRS), is smooth, non-monotonic, and bounded. Notably, the bounded property of SRS distinguishes itself from most state-of-the-art activation functions. In contrast to ReLU, SRS can adaptively adjust the output by a pair of independent trainable parameters to capture negative information and provide zero-mean property, which leading not only to better generalization performance, but also to faster learning speed. It also avoids and rectifies the output distribution to be scattered in the non-negative real number space, making it more compatible with batch normalization (BN) and less sensitive to initialization. In experiments, we evaluated SRS on deep networks applied to a variety of tasks, including image classification, machine translation and generative modelling. Our SRS matches or exceeds models with ReLU and other state-of-the-art nonlinearities, showing that the proposed activation function is generalized and can achieve high performance across tasks. Ablation study further verified the compatibility with BN and self-adaptability for different initialization.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Soft-Root-Sign (SRS), a smooth, non-monotonic, bounded activation function meant to replace piecewise-linear ReLU, and evaluates it across image classification, machine translation, and generative modeling. In the generative part it tests SRS against other nonlinearities inside an i-ResNet flow on 2D toy densities ("two moons", "pinwheel", "eight gaussians"), reporting that continuous/smooth units (SRS, ELU) model multi-modal and discontinuous distributions better than ReLU-type piecewise linear units, which lead to unstable optimization in the flow setting.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's core problem is the difficulty of *leveraging piecewise linear units' benefits in the generative context*. This paper does not solve that: it does not make piecewise linear units work better in generative models, but instead substitutes a smooth, bounded, non-piecewise activation. The generative evidence is limited to a qualitative comparison on small 2D toy densities with one flow architecture (i-ResNet, brute-force log-determinant), without real-scale generative tasks (GANs, VAEs, image density estimation) or an analysis of why piecewise linear units fail in generative settings beyond observing unstable optimization. Consequently, the specific problem of benefiting from piecewise linear units in generative models—rather than abandoning them—remains open, and even the proposed workaround is only demonstrated under limited conditions.

paper.title: Implicit Manifold Learning on Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: This paper raises an implicit manifold learning perspective in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), by studying how the support of the learned distribution, modelled as a submanifold $\mathcal{M}_θ$, perfectly match with $\mathcal{M}_{r}$, the support of the real data distribution. We show that optimizing Jensen-Shannon divergence forces $\mathcal{M}_θ$ to perfectly match with $\mathcal{M}_{r}$, while optimizing Wasserstein distance does not. On the other hand, by comparing the gradients of the Jensen-Shannon divergence and the Wasserstein distances ($W_1$ and $W_2^2$) in their primal forms, we conjecture that Wasserstein $W_2^2$ may enjoy desirable properties such as reduced mode collapse. It is therefore interesting to design new distances that inherit the best from both distances.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper studies JS and Wasserstein distances in GANs when real and generated distributions are supported on low-dimensional submanifolds. Its main results characterize support alignment: optimizing JSD below log 2 forces positive overlap between model and data supports (MCS^α > 0), whereas W_p does not force such alignment (distributions with measure-zero overlap are dense in any W_p ball). It also compares generator gradients of W1, W2^2, and JSD with respect to mode diversity. These contributions concern geometric support matching and mode collapse, not the (un)definedness or discontinuity of KL/JS/TV as cost functions that is the substance of the stated gap.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — that KL can be undefined/infinite and JS/TV discontinuous when distributions are supported on low-dimensional manifolds, making them unsuitable cost functions — is not tackled. The paper instead assumes the degeneracy away: Assumptions A1/A2 require the distributions to be absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue/Hausdorff measure on their k-dimensional supports (with positive measure), and Assumption A3 (equal, full-dimensional supports / Gaussian convolution) is introduced explicitly "to insure KL divergence is finite." No alternative cost function that is well-behaved on low-dimensional manifolds is proposed or validated; the paper itself only suggests designing such distances as future work ("It is therefore interesting to design new distances..."). Moreover, it argues JSD has a desirable alignment property in this regime, which is a different research question from whether KL/JS/TV are sensible, continuous, well-defined divergences for manifold-supported data.
